strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: adapting BALD-style epistemic uncertainty estimation from active learning to attention maps for noise-seed selection in video diffusion, without any retraining or external priors.

Clean theoretical formalization, including a proof (Proposition 1) that the proposed BANSA score vanishes exactly when stochastic attention samples agree, giving a principled interpretation of the metric.

Practical efficiency considerations are carefully engineered: Bernoulli-masked attention to approximate K stochastic passes in a single forward pass, restriction to an early denoising step, and correlation-based layer truncation to reduce compute, yielding modest reported overhead (8%/13%).

Reasonably thorough ablation studies: comparison of acquisition functions (random, entropy, BANSA with dropout vs. Bernoulli masking), effect of ensemble size K, effect of noise pool size M, and a sanity-check 'reversed BANSA' experiment showing that selecting the highest-uncertainty seed degrades quality.

Evaluated on two model scales (CogVideoX-2B and -5B) with the standard VBench benchmark, plus multiple qualitative figures across diverse prompts, and the paper candidly discusses a failure case and limitation (Figure 7).
weaknesses: The absolute quantitative gains on VBench are small (e.g., quality +0.17 to +0.48 points, total score +0.19 to +0.63 out of 100), and no variance/significance analysis (e.g., across multiple runs or seeds pools) is provided to establish that these gains are statistically meaningful rather than noise.

The method is only validated on a single model family (CogVideoX 2B/5B); no experiments on other T2V backbones (e.g., different attention architectures, DiT-based models beyond CogVideoX) are shown despite claims of 'generalizability across various text-to-video architectures.'

No direct quantitative comparison against the frequency-prior baselines (FreeInit, FreqPrior) that the paper explicitly positions itself against; these are omitted with a justification that re-implementation is costly, which weakens the empirical case for superiority claimed in the abstract/intro.

The claimed inference overhead (8%/13%) is computed only in terms of denoising-step count for the extra uncertainty-estimation step, but selecting the best of M=10 candidate seeds implicitly requires forwarding through the noise pool; the reported overhead figures and their derivation are not fully transparent, raising concern that total practical cost (including noise-pool evaluation across candidates) could be understated.

No comparison against simpler non-uncertainty selection heuristics (e.g., ranking candidate seeds by a lightweight proxy quality score, CLIP-based text-video alignment, or a trained discriminator) to demonstrate that the specific Bayesian/attention-entropy formulation is necessary rather than any reasonable seed-ranking criterion.

Evaluation relies solely on automatic VBench metrics; no human/user study is conducted to corroborate the qualitative claims of improved visual quality and semantic alignment, despite substantial reliance on qualitative figures for the paper's narrative.

The theoretical grounding is somewhat loose: the paper acknowledges in a footnote that 'BANSA is not derived from a formal Bayesian posterior,' and the Bernoulli-masked approximation is admitted to potentially be biased due to the nonlinearity of entropy, undermining the 'principled' framing emphasized throughout.

strengths: The core idea of repurposing BALD-style epistemic uncertainty estimation to the attention maps of video diffusion models for inference-time noise seed selection is a reasonably novel and intuitively motivated adaptation of active learning concepts to generative inference-time scaling.

The Bernoulli-masked attention approximation and the correlation-based layer-truncation heuristic are practical engineering solutions that keep the method's overhead low (8-13% extra inference time), which is attractive relative to multi-pass frequency-prior baselines like FreeInit/FreePrior.

The paper includes a reasonably thorough set of ablations (acquisition function comparison, ensemble size K, noise pool size M, reversed-criterion sanity check, full-layer vs. truncated BANSA, temporal scope) and an honest limitations/failure-case discussion (Figure 7).
Proposition 1 gives a simple theoretical justification (via Jensen's inequality) for why minimizing BANSA corresponds to attention consistency across stochastic samples.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single model family (CogVideoX-2B/5B); despite claims of "generalizability across architectures" and "various T2V architectures," no other backbone (e.g., Wan, LTX-Video, Hunyuan, Open-Sora, which are all cited) is tested, so generalization claims are unsupported.

The reported quantitative gains are small in absolute terms (total VBench score +0.63 for 2B, +0.19/+0.25 for 5B), with no variance/confidence intervals or statistical significance testing provided despite generating thousands of videos; it is unclear whether these differences are meaningful beyond noise.

No direct quantitative comparison against the most relevant prior noise-selection/prior-based baselines (FreeInit, FreePrior, PYoCo, FreeNoise) is actually performed; the paper argues they are impractical to reproduce and only discusses a rough 3x/200% cost estimate, which weakens the central claim of superiority/efficiency over prior work.

No human evaluation or qualitative user study is used to corroborate the automated VBench metric improvements, which are known to be imperfect proxies for perceptual quality, especially given the small quantitative deltas.

The main paper's BANSA formulation (entropy of mean minus mean of entropies, i.e., negative mutual information) is sign-inverted relative to the appendix's actual implementation (BALD-style, mean of entropies minus entropy of mean); while the authors clarify this post hoc, it indicates sloppy presentation and could confuse reproducibility.

The theoretical contribution (Proposition 1) is a direct, essentially textbook consequence of Jensen's inequality applied to entropy's concavity, offering limited additional insight beyond restating the known BALD rationale.

The method only aids seed selection, not generation quality itself (as acknowledged in Figure 7/Section 6); given the modest measured gains, the practical significance of the contribution is questionable.

Discussion of cited learned/noise-optimization methods (InitNO, ReNO, Tino-Edit, "Good Seed") in the introduction is not empirically compared against, leaving the positioning against closely related inference-time noise-selection work incomplete.

The qualitative figures, while illustrative, are cherry-picked single examples per prompt and cannot substitute for quantitative evidence of consistent improvement, especially given the small aggregate gains in Table 1.

strengths: Proposes a conceptually appealing and novel idea: using internal attention-based uncertainty (rather than externally designed frequency priors) to select high-quality initial noise seeds for text-to-video diffusion, avoiding retraining or auxiliary models.

Provides a principled formulation grounded in a BALD-style Bayesian active learning framework, including a formal Proposition (with proof) characterizing when the BANSA score is zero, adding some theoretical grounding.

Introduces a practical Bernoulli-masked approximation for computing multiple stochastic attention samples in a single forward pass, plus a correlation-based layer-truncation strategy, both aimed at making the method inference-efficient.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies: comparison against random/entropy baselines, effect of ensemble size K, noise pool size M, full-layer vs. truncated BANSA, temporal scope of BANSA computation, and a sanity-check reversed-criterion experiment that supports the direction of the score.

Evaluation uses a large number of generated videos (4,730 per configuration) on the standard VBench suite, and reports both quantitative and qualitative comparisons; the paper is transparent about a failure case and limitation (Figure 7, Section 6).
weaknesses: The quantitative gains are quite small in absolute terms (VBench total score improves by only 0.63 and 0.25 points out of 100 for the two backbones), and no variance/error bars or repeated-run statistics are reported, making it hard to judge statistical significance of the improvement.

Both evaluated backbones (CogVideoX-2B and 5B) come from the same model family; despite claims of "generalizability across architectures," no fundamentally different T2V backbone (e.g., a different architecture/tokenizer family) is tested, limiting evidence for broad applicability.

The paper claims ANSE is "orthogonal and can be combined" with FreeInit/FreqPrior, but no empirical combination or direct quantitative comparison against these closely related baselines is provided; they are simply omitted citing cost, which weakens the positioning relative to prior work.

Evaluation relies solely on the automatic VBench metric; no human/user study is included to validate that the modest score improvements translate to perceptible quality gains, especially given the failure case shown in Figure 7 where low BANSA score does not guarantee good generation.

The claimed 8%/13% inference overhead for evaluating a pool of 10 candidate seeds (each requiring partial forward passes with K=10 attention samples) is not clearly justified/broken down, leaving the computational accounting somewhat opaque.

Use of the term "Bayesian" is acknowledged in a footnote as not being derived from a formal Bayesian posterior, which is a fairly loose theoretical framing for a paper whose method name and core acquisition function are built around this terminology.

strengths: Proposes a genuinely useful and practical idea: using internal attention-based epistemic uncertainty (via a BALD-inspired acquisition function, BANSA) to select noise seeds in T2V diffusion, avoiding the external frequency priors and costly full sampling passes required by prior work (FreeInit, FreqPrior).

Efficient engineering: a Bernoulli-masked single-pass approximation of the K-sample BANSA score plus a layer-truncation scheme (via cumulative correlation analysis) keeps inference overhead low (~8-15%) compared to competing noise-refinement methods that incur ~100-200% overhead.

Broad empirical validation across many and recent backbones (AnimateDiff, CogVideoX-2B/5B, HunyuanVideo, Wan2.1 1.3B/14B) and even a post-RL/DPO-tuned model (JPOC-2B), suggesting reasonably general applicability.

Extensive and well-designed ablations: acquisition-function comparison, ensemble size K, noise pool size M, Bernoulli masking probability p, a reversed-BANSA sanity check, self- vs. cross-attention analysis, CFG-scale interaction, equivalent-compute-budget comparison, and bootstrap confidence-interval statistical validation.

Interpretability analyses (cross-prompt behavior, intra-prompt attention consistency, latent trajectory variation) and a correlation study (BANSA vs. VBench metrics) that support the claimed mechanism, along with a modest human preference study.
Honest discussion of limitations, including an explicit failure case where a low-BANSA seed still yields an unnatural video.
weaknesses: Absolute quantitative gains are often small (e.g., VBench total score improves by roughly 0.6-1.4 points on 100-point scales for several backbones; some individual metrics even appear to slightly regress, e.g., Subject/Background Consistency for HunyuanVideo in Table 5), so the practical significance of the improvement is somewhat unclear despite the reported confidence intervals.

The theoretical contribution (Proposition 1) is a direct, low-novelty consequence of Jensen's inequality already implicit in the BALD framework; calling the approach 'principled' may overstate the technical depth beyond adapting an existing acquisition function to a new modality.

Important recent/relevant baselines for seed/noise selection (e.g., reward-based noise optimization such as ReNO, or other noise-seed search works cited in the intro) are not empirically compared against; FreqPrior/FreeInit comparisons are restricted only to AnimateDiff, limiting the strength of the comparative evaluation on modern backbones.

The claim that layer truncation and seed selection add 'no runtime cost' (Sec 3.3) is inconsistent with the reported 8-15% inference overhead in the main experiments; this creates some internal inconsistency in how the efficiency claims are framed.

Model-specific hyperparameters (cutoff layer d*, Bernoulli p, K, M) are tuned per backbone via correlation analysis against VBench-related quality scores, which somewhat undercuts the 'plug-and-play, training-free' framing and raises a mild concern about calibration on the same benchmark used for final evaluation.

The human study is relatively small in scale (30 prompts, 12 evaluators, 4 backbones) and mainly corroborates automated VBench metrics rather than providing independent strong evidence of perceptual quality gains.
Minor presentation issues (inconsistent naming such as 'Wanx' vs 'Wan', 'HunyangVideo' vs 'HunyuanVideo', a typo 'signicance') suggest the manuscript could benefit from more careful proofreading.

strengths: Introduces a training-free, model-aware acquisition function (BANSA) for noise-seed selection in T2V diffusion, motivated by a clean adaptation of the BALD principle to attention maps, with a formal zero-condition proposition and proof (via Jensen's inequality).

Broad empirical coverage across many backbones (AnimateDiff, CogVideoX-2B/5B, HunyuanVideo, Wan2.1 1.3B/14B) and even a post-RL preference-aligned model (IPOC-2B), suggesting the approach is architecture-agnostic.

Extensive ablations (acquisition function variants, ensemble size K, noise pool size M, Bernoulli masking probability, layer truncation depth, temporal scope, CFG interaction, equivalent-compute baseline, reversed-criterion sanity check) demonstrate a reasonably thorough exploration of the design space.

Efficient approximation (single-pass Bernoulli-masked attention, early-step, truncated-layer scoring) keeps inference overhead low (roughly +8% to +15%) compared to prior noise-refinement baselines like FreeInit/FreqPrior, which need full extra denoising passes (+100-200% overhead).
Includes a human preference study and correlation analysis (Pearson correlation between BANSA and VBench metrics) as complementary evidence beyond automatic metrics.
Method is shown to be compatible/orthogonal with existing frequency-prior methods (FreqPrior), yielding further gains when combined.
weaknesses: Effect sizes are often small and, for some backbones (e.g., HunyuanVideo in Table 5), the reported metrics are nearly identical between vanilla and +Ours (differences in the third/fourth decimal), which undercuts the claim of 'consistent' and practically meaningful improvement across all backbones.

The correlation analysis (Fig. 5b, Section on 'Analysis on correlation with actual quality') that supports the core validity of BANSA is computed post-hoc on the same type of data used to design/tune the method, raising circularity concerns rather than providing independent causal validation.

Missing an important and natural baseline: selecting seeds using a cheap off-the-shelf proxy (e.g., predicted x0 at step 1 via Tweedie's formula scored by a CLIP/aesthetic/reward model) rather than attention entropy. Without this comparison it is unclear whether the specific attention-based uncertainty signal is necessary, versus any cheap early-stage quality proxy achieving similar gains.

Baseline noise-refinement comparisons (FreeInit, FreqPrior) are only run on AnimateDiff, with the justification that they 'lack official support' on other backbones — this seems avoidable since these are generic frequency-domain operations on noise, and the omission weakens the comparative evaluation on the paper's main claimed contribution (efficiency vs. prior noise-init methods).

The cross-prompt/intra-prompt analyses in Section 4 (Tables 1-3) are based on very limited samples (single seeds, 100 prompts with small pairwise-distance deltas) and read as illustrative anecdotes rather than statistically rigorous evidence of the claimed prompt-dependent behavior.

The 'Bayesian' framing is a loose analogy to BALD; the paper itself concedes in a footnote that it uses 'Bayesian' only in the sense of epistemic-uncertainty estimation without a true posterior, which makes the prominent title/abstract framing ('Bayesian Active Noise Selection') somewhat oversold relative to the underlying heuristic (Bernoulli-masked entropy disagreement).
Limited discussion of failure modes (only a single qualitative failure case in Fig. 6) and no quantitative characterization of how often BANSA selection fails or underperforms random selection.

Numerous typos and inconsistent formatting throughout (e.g., 'HunyangVideo', 'statistical siganceance', 'Wanx' vs 'Wan' inconsistencies) suggest the manuscript would benefit from a careful proofreading pass.

strengths: Introduces BANSA, a principled BALD-style acquisition function operating in attention space rather than external frequency priors, with a clean theoretical zero-condition result (Proposition 1) tying the score to attention agreement/consistency.

Efficient practical approximation: Bernoulli-masked single-pass stochastic sampling, early-denoising-step evaluation, and correlation-based layer truncation together keep inference overhead to roughly +8% to +15%, in sharp contrast to prior noise-refinement baselines (FreeInit, FreqPrior) that require repeated full sampling passes and incur >100% overhead.

Broad empirical coverage across diverse T2V backbones spanning U-Net (AnimateDiff), DiT (CogVideoX-2B/5B), and modern large-scale models (Wan2.1, HunyuanVideo, Wan2.1-14B), plus demonstrated plug-and-play compatibility with FreqPrior and a post-RL/DPO-tuned model (IPOC-2B), suggesting good generality.

Extensive ablations (acquisition function variants, ensemble size K, noise pool size M, Bernoulli masking probability, layer/attention-type analysis, CFG interaction, equivalent-compute-budget control, reversed-criterion sanity check) that collectively support the design choices and the causal role of BANSA in quality gains.

Reasonable statistical rigor (confidence intervals over multiple runs) and a blinded human preference study that corroborates automatic VBench improvements; correlation analysis (Fig. 5b) directly links BANSA scores to standard quality metrics.

Honest discussion of limitations, including a shown failure case where low-BANSA seeds still yield unnatural content, acknowledging the method only selects seeds rather than altering the generative trajectory.
weaknesses: No comparison against a natural and important baseline: best-of-N seed selection using an existing off-the-shelf reward/quality predictor (e.g., aesthetic or CLIP-based scorer) instead of BANSA; without this, it is unclear how much of the benefit comes specifically from the attention-uncertainty formulation versus simply reranking multiple candidates by any quality proxy.

Comparison with FreqPrior (the closest recent noise-prior baseline) is only conducted on AnimateDiff due to lack of official support elsewhere, weakening the generality claims for the combined method on modern DiT/MMDiT backbones.

Some quantitative gains are numerically small (e.g., Table 7 acquisition-function ablation, several VBench sub-metrics in Tables 4-5), and while confidence intervals are reported, the practical significance of some improvements (a few tenths of a point) is not strongly argued beyond statistical presence.

The overall novelty is largely an application/engineering adaptation of the well-established BALD principle to attention maps in diffusion; the core conceptual leap is modest, with most contribution residing in the efficient approximation engineering rather than a fundamentally new uncertainty formulation.

Cost of generating and partially denoising a full noise pool (M=10) per prompt is not discussed in the context of amortized/production use cases where a single high-quality seed is needed repeatedly, nor benchmarked against cheaper alternatives that might use fewer or adaptively pruned candidates.

Minor presentation issues: inconsistent figure/table captions (e.g., "HunyangVideo" vs "HunyuanVideo"), a typo ("significane"), and some qualitative figures lack quantitative summary, relying on visual inspection alone.
